summary:
Cyprus is a workable destination for trans visitors. There is no legal restriction on gender presentation, no facility or bathroom law of the kind enacted elsewhere in the region, and no border obstacle beyond the standard entry rules that apply to any European Union member state. Tourist infrastructure is Western-standard and accustomed to international visitors.

The statutory framework contains explicit gender-identity protections in criminal law. Law 87(I)/2015 makes public incitement to violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity a criminal offence; the underlying penal code amendment dates from October 2013 and carries up to three years' imprisonment and/or a fine of €5,000. Law 31(I)/2017 provides that prejudice-based motivation is an aggravating factor in sentencing for hate crimes. Law 39(I)/2023 bans and criminalises conversion practices.

No legal gender recognition procedure is in force. A gender recognition bill was approved by the Council of Ministers in September 2022 and received its first parliamentary reading in November 2022, and it remained pending as of 2024. In its 2019 national report to the UN review process Cyprus stated that legislation allowing correction of registered sex for adults and minors, requiring only a Registrar decision with no prior medical intervention or psychiatric reports, was in preparation. A visitor whose documents were updated abroad should expect the mismatch between passport and other records to stand, since the domestic route is not yet open.

Gender identity is absent from the grounds of general equal-treatment law, so a discrimination claim outside the criminal and workplace spheres has no statutory basis on that ground, and no national anti-homophobia action plan exists. Workplace protections on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds were added in 2004.

Detention carries a documented institutional risk. Prison guards received two days of LGBTI+ training in April 2023, introduced after complaints of anti-LGBTI harassment reached the Ombudswoman.

The island is divided, and the northern part of Cyprus runs its own gender-recognition process on a self-determination basis without psychiatric or surgical gatekeeping, explicitly including recognition of non-binary identities. The framework documented by Queer Cyprus Association applies there independently of the stalled bill in the south.
tangentialFactors:
Cyprus accepted all eight sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics recommendations put to it at the 32nd session of the UN Universal Periodic Review Working Group in January 2019. The state response recorded since then is uneven: the hate-speech offence was delivered, while the gender-identity discrimination ground and trans-specific legislation were not.

The European Commission's network of legal experts reviewed transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives in Cyprus in reports covering 2019 and 2023, including the gender-identity aspects of the framework. The inventory does not itemise their specific findings on trans issues.

The Council of Europe's Commission against Racism and Intolerance has urged that gender identity be written into the prohibited grounds of discrimination, a recommendation that matches the current gap in equal-treatment law. Cyprus joined the Equal Rights Coalition as its 40th member in August 2018.

Queer Cyprus Association frames trans and gender-diverse rights as the outstanding implementation issue of the current review cycle, with the September 2022 recognition bill as the step that would close it. Comparable jurisdictions in the region have moved to self-declaration models, which leaves Cyprus behind its immediate peers on documentation.
localsOnly:
Queer Cyprus Association operates a confidential psychosocial and legal support line seven days a week, covering identity matters, employment, family, shelter, health and military-service issues. It is the principal point of contact for residents facing institutional friction.

Residents seeking to change legal gender have no domestic procedure to apply to while the 2022 bill remains pending, and general discrimination complaints cannot be brought on a gender-identity ground because that ground is not written into equal-treatment law.

People subject to detention or military service face the conditions that prompted the April 2023 training of prison guards, introduced after anti-LGBTI harassment complaints to the Ombudswoman. Two days of instruction is the extent of the documented corrective measure.

Residents in the northern part of the island can obtain recognition of their gender, including non-binary identities, through the separate process operating there on self-determination terms.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the gender recognition bill approved in September 2022 has been enacted since the 2024 reporting date is unresolved in the sources supplied; the latest status in the inventory is first parliamentary reading in November 2022 and pending status in 2024.

Whether gender identity has since been added to the grounds of general equal-treatment law, and whether a national anti-homophobia action plan has been adopted, are not sourced and remain open.

The enforcement record of the 2013 incitement offence as extended in 2015, and of the 2017 aggravating-factor provision, is not sourced; no prosecutions or sentences are documented in the inventory.

The precise scope of the 2004 workplace protections, in particular whether they name gender identity expressly or reach beyond employment, is not detailed in the sources.

How a recognition certificate issued in the northern part of the island is treated by authorities in the south, and the documentary requirements for crossing between the two, are not sourced.

The specific gender-identity findings of the two European Commission legal experts' reports are not itemised in the inventory and would need to be read from the reports themselves.
